value.body: Tests printed circuit boards and finished electronic products in a factory to check they work as designed. Electronics manufacturing and assembly companies hire for this role. The day is spent at test stations — running test programs, finding faults, sending boards for rework and logging results.

items.label: Typical entry
items.value: B.Sc Electronics, a diploma in electronics, or ITI
items.note: Some plants hire B.Sc graduates as trainees

items.label: Common tools
items.value: Test jigs, multimeters, oscilloscopes, soldering stations

items.label: Standards followed
items.value: IPC workmanship standards and ESD-safe handling

items.label: Jobs in electronics manufacturing
items.source: Industry estimates cited by MeitY (as reported)

value.title: How you get in
value.body: Freshers join as trainees or operators-turned-technicians in electronics manufacturing units, often through campus drives, walk-ins or apprenticeship schemes in industrial areas. Interviews check basic electronics, component identification and soldering. Shift work is usual.

value.title: At a glance
items: Growth path: technician → senior technician → test or quality engineer (often with further study).
Work is shift-based and on the factory floor.
Experience with test programs can lead into test engineering roles.

value.title: Domestic electronics production
value.note: Value of goods produced, not employment; mobile phones make up a large share. Figures rounded.
value.source: MeitY figures in Parliament replies and PIB (as reported)
